Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Open VSX evil-twin extension exfiltration to mangorbit[.]com C2 infrastructure AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to mangorbit.com or its subdomains (pulse, pulse2, api, cb.*), the single exfiltration domain shared by all 77 counterfeit Open VSX developer-tool extensions. Because the domain was registered 11 days before the campaign and is used exclusively by these malicious packages, any contact is high-fidelity evidence of an installed evil-twin extension. Rationale: Anchors on mangorbit.com (and pulse/pulse2/api/cb subdomains) — the single exfil domain Manifold links all 77 packages through, registered 2026-07-15, 11 days pre-campaign. `has "mangorbit"` token-matches every subdomain including the randomized cb.* ones. Domain is single-source (Manifold/BleepingComputer) but its exclusivity and fresh registration make any contact high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/77-open-vsx-extensions-found-harvesting-developer-info/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/glassworm-supply-chain-attack-abuses-72.html • https://socket.dev/blog/glassworm-sleeper-extensions-activated-on-open-vsx
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1176.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or detonation VM resolving the IOC during sample triage
  • Threat-intel enrichment host (urlscan/VirusTotal-style scanner) auto-resolving the domain from an IOC feed
  • SOAR playbook performing automated IOC enrichment/lookup of mangorbit.com
  • Post-takedown sinkhole/NXDOMAIN attempts still generating DNS log entries after the domain was pulled 2026-08-03
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving/connecting host and the InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm it is a code editor (Code.exe/Cursor.exe/node.exe) and not a sandbox/TI-enrichment host. Pull the developer's installed Open VSX extension list and match IDs against Manifold's report. 2) Contain: block mangorbit.com at DNS/proxy/firewall org-wide; on the affected host uninstall the counterfeit extension and remove it from workspace .vscode/extensions.json recommendation configs. 3) Hunt: sweep all dev endpoints for the same domain, review .git remote hosts / CI tokens (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Buildkite, CircleCI, Codespaces, Gitpod) that were readable in exposed workspaces, and rotate any CI identifiers that could have been profiled.

| where RemoteUrl has "mangorbit"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "mangorbit" | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, Source="DNS", EventVendor, EventProduct),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName has "mangorbit" or RequestURL has "mangorbit" | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), DnsQueryTypeName="", Source="Proxy", EventVendor=DeviceVendor, EventProduct=DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Code editor / node extension-host resolving mangorbit[.]com (evil-twin attribution) AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates hosts that both run a VS Code-family editor (Code/Cursor/Windsurf/VSCodium/node extension host) and resolve mangorbit.com, attributing the exfiltration to the malicious extension running inside the editor rather than a coincidental IOC hit. Scopes the alert to developer workstations and confirms the extension-host process as the initiator, and covers the DNS-based fallback channel the malware uses when hardcoded infrastructure is unreachable. Rationale: Ties the mangorbit.com contact to the editor extension-host process (Code/Cursor/Windsurf/VSCodium/node) — the article states the payload runs inside the extension host and sends data ~4-5s after activation, and falls back to a DNS TXT lookup for a replacement URL when hardcoded infra is down. Process attribution both raises fidelity over the pure-network hit and scopes the hunt to developer workstations. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/77-open-vsx-extensions-found-harvesting-developer-info/ • https://socket.dev/blog/glassworm-loader-hits-open-vsx-via-suspected-developer-account-compromise
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568.002 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually resolving/testing the mangorbit.com IOC from a terminal inside VS Code
  • Security team running Manifold's own detection/verification script from a dev workstation
  • node.exe on a build agent resolving the domain during an unrelated dependency fetch that a proxy rewrote
  • Post-takedown NXDOMAIN retries logged from the extension host before the extension is removed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a code-editor/extension host and enumerate that user's Open VSX extensions (version 0.0.1 low-version counterfeits, unrelated publisher namespaces impersonating AMD/Azure/Salesforce/Hyperledger/LEGO Education/IOTA). 2) Contain: uninstall the offending extension, purge it from the host and any shared workspace .vscode config, and DNS-block mangorbit.com. 3) Hunt: check for randomized subdomains under cb.mangorbit.com and DNS TXT queries (fallback-channel resolution) from the same host, and review which Git/CI metadata (remote hosts, org, configured-email domain, branch, HEAD hash, CI/cloud-dev identifiers) the extension could have profiled.

| where RemoteUrl has "mangorbit"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","vscodium.exe","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("extension.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

128 Seconds to disruption: Microsoft Defender stops ransomware at QNET

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-08-04 9 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Defender automatically isolated a compromised QNET endpoint in 128 seconds, stopping a multi-stage attack before the payload could persist or spread. The post 128 Seconds to disruption: Microsoft Defender stops ransomware at QNET appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1057 T1059 T1071.001 T1105 T1112 T1190 T1204 T1204.002 T1218.005 T1486
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected
Phase 2
Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected
Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] mshta.exe launched with inline http/https URL argument
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] mshta.exe spawning command interpreter or secondary LOLBin
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RunMRU registry write launching mshta / URL / PowerShell (ClickFix-style user persistence) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] mshta.exe outbound connection to public host (remote HTA C2 retrieval) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
mshta.exe outbound connection to public host (remote HTA C2 retrieval) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the QNET-style chain where signed mshta.exe reaches out to attacker infrastructure to pull a second-stage payload. Fires on mshta.exe as the initiating process for any connection to a public IP — mshta has no legitimate reason to egress to the internet in most environments. Rationale: Anchored on the article's stated behaviour: 'mshta.exe process contacted an attacker-controlled URL and retrieved a second-stage payload' (Table 2 maps this to T1071.001). mshta egress to public IPs is near-zero in benign use. Corroborated by Sigma proc_creation_win_mshta_http and MITRE T1218.005. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_mshta_http/ • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/techniques/mshta/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that legitimately deploy signed internal HTA files hosted on an internal web server (would resolve to private IPs, excluded here)
  • Vendor management/monitoring agents that shell out to mshta against an on-prem console
  • Software installers that briefly invoke mshta against a vendor CDN
  • Security tooling / EDR test harnesses running atomic-red-team T1218.005 tests
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".internal.contoso.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the mshta InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl; check whether the destination is newly-registered or has any threat-intel hits, and identify the parent that launched mshta. 2) Contain: if the destination is unknown/malicious, isolate the device (Defender attack-disruption may already have) and block the IP/domain at the proxy. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to DeviceRegistryEvents for RunMRU writes and DeviceProcessEvents for child processes spawned by mshta within the surrounding 5 minutes; sweep the org for any other host that contacted the same RemoteIP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)

mshta.exe launched with inline http/https URL argument AIDelivery High
Hunts direct invocation of mshta.exe with a remote URL on the command line — the exact delivery primitive in the QNET incident where a malicious file caused mshta to fetch and execute a remote HTA. Complements the network UC by catching the command-line intent even when egress telemetry is missing. Rationale: Directly implements the article's delivery step (T1218.005 + T1204.002 in Table 2): mshta.exe proxying execution of attacker-controlled remote content. A remote URL on the mshta command line is one of the highest-fidelity LOLBin signatures. Matches the widely-deployed Sigma proc_creation_win_mshta_http logic. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_mshta_http/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/e13ceade-b673-4d34-adc4-4d9c01729753/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise apps that legitimately package HTA UIs and pass an internal http URL (whitelist the internal host)
  • IT deployment scripts using mshta to render a remote help/onboarding page
  • Atomic Red Team / purple-team T1218.005 execution during scheduled testing
  • Rare third-party software updaters that stage content via mshta
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://helpdesk.contoso.com","https://intranet.contoso.com"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full mshta command line and the URL, and identify the parent process (was it a browser download, email client, or Explorer opening a downloaded file?). 2) Contain: block the URL/domain, quarantine the originating file if identifiable, and isolate the host if the URL is unknown/malicious. 3) Hunt: check DeviceFileEvents for the file the user opened and any payload mshta wrote to disk; look for RunMRU registry writes and mshta child processes on the same host and across the fleet contacting the same domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","ftp://")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","ftp://")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Remotely Hosted HTA Executed via Mshta.EXE

references:

RunMRU registry write launching mshta / URL / PowerShell (ClickFix-style user persistence) AIInstallation High
Hunts the RunMRU registry interaction the article flags as user-level persistence — the HKCU Run-dialog MRU key populated with a command that launches mshta, an http URL, or PowerShell. This is the classic ClickFix pattern where a user is socially engineered into pasting an attacker command into the Run box. Rationale: Implements the article's stated persistence artifact verbatim: 'Suspicious RunMRU-related registry interaction indicated attempted user-level persistence' (Table 2 -> T1112). External research confirms RunMRU (HKCU\...\Explorer\RunMRU) storing a URL/mshta/PowerShell command is the ClickFix fileless pattern. Falcon left empty: FDR AsepValueUpdate covers autostart ASEPs, not the non-autostart RunMRU key. Cross-checked against: • https://undercodetesting.com/detecting-clickfix-malware-via-runmru-registry-key-in-microsoft-defender/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/e13ceade-b673-4d34-adc4-4d9c01729753/
ATT&CKT1112 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A power user or sysadmin legitimately typing a PowerShell or UNC command into the Run dialog
  • Help-desk staff pasting an internal http URL into Run to open a web resource
  • Developers launching local dev servers (http://localhost) via the Run box
  • Software that programmatically seeds RunMRU during setup (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-deploy","helpdesk-admin") and RegistryValueData has "http://localhost")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full RegistryValueData command that was written to RunMRU and determine whether a matching process (mshta/powershell) actually executed on the host afterward. 2) Contain: if the command is malicious, isolate the host and disable/notify the affected user account; capture the command as an IOC. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for the exact command executing, and DeviceNetworkEvents for the URL contacted; sweep other users/hosts for the same RunMRU string (indicates a broader social-engineering / ClickFix campaign).
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has "Explorer\\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","http","powershell",".hta","cmd /c")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has "Explorer\\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","http","powershell",".hta","cmd /c")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Suspicious Command in RunMRU Registry Key (ClickFix)

mshta.exe spawning command interpreter or secondary LOLBin AIExploitation High
Hunts the 'suspicious command execution' the article observed once the second-stage HTA ran under mshta — mshta.exe as parent of cmd/powershell/wscript/cscript/rundll32/regsvr32. A signed HTA host spawning a scripting engine is a strong post-exploitation execution signal. Rationale: Implements the article's 'suspicious command execution' and T1059 mapping (Table 2): the HTA-delivered script executed through mshta.exe, enabling follow-on commands. mshta parenting a scripting engine is rare in benign use and marks the pivot from delivery to hands-on execution. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/ • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/techniques/mshta/
ATT&CKT1059 T1218.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal HTA applications that shell out to cmd/wscript for legitimate automation
  • Software installers packaged as HTA that call regsvr32/rundll32 during setup
  • Admin diagnostic HTAs that launch PowerShell for system queries
  • Purple-team T1218.005 chains during authorized testing
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "C:\\Program Files\\ContosoLOB\\app.hta")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the child process command line (decode any base64/encoded PowerShell) and the parent mshta command line to determine what the HTA instructed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and preserve the mshta parent and any dropped files for forensics. 3) Hunt: enumerate everything the child spawned (grandchildren), check DeviceNetworkEvents for C2 from the child, DeviceRegistryEvents for RunMRU/Run-key persistence, and DeviceFileEvents for payloads written to Temp/AppData; sweep the fleet for the same mshta->child pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

Malicious csvFile data URI with Python/JS breakout posted to Flowise /api/v1/prediction AIExploitation Medium
Hunts POST requests to Flowise's public /api/v1/prediction/<id> endpoint carrying a csvFile data URI whose base64 segment contains Python/JS breakout tokens (import js, js.eval, child_process, __import__). Distinguishes malicious CSVAgent abuse from benign base64 CSV uploads by requiring the interpreter-escape strings the exploit needs. Rationale: Uses the article-specific endpoint path /api/v1/prediction/ (WHITELIST_URLS, reachable unauthenticated) plus the exact breakout tokens the exploit interpolates (import js, js.eval, child_process, __import__, and the read_pickle variant from the sibling advisory). Request-body inspection requires WAF/proxy full-capture; Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty as those sources do not ship HTTP bodies. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv/ • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate CSVAgent usage: analysts uploading a real base64-encoded CSV data URI to a prediction flow (no breakout tokens present)
  • Security scanners / DAST tools probing the prediction endpoint with test payloads
  • Internal red-team or pentest validation of CVE-2026-69264
  • WAF already blocking the request (still logged as attempt)
Suppression filter
| where not(Message has_any ("nessus","qualys","burpsuite","acunetix") or RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Burp"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body for the flagged prediction call; confirm the csvFile base64 segment decodes to Python containing js.eval / import('child_process') / read_pickle rather than legitimate CSV bytes. Note source IP and whether the chatflow has an apikeyid set (unauthenticated = higher risk). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, disable the exposed chatflow, and confirm Flowise is patched to >=3.1.3; if pre-patch, take the instance offline. 3) Hunt: on the Flowise host, pivot to child processes of node.exe within the same window (UC2/UC3) and search for dropped files (e.g. proof.txt) or outbound C2 from the node process.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/prediction/"
| where Message has_any ("csvFile","data:","base64,","import js","js.eval","child_process","__import__","read_pickle","u002c") or RequestContext has_any ("csvFile","js.eval","child_process","__import__")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise Node.js process spawning shell/interpreter child (CSVAgent RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Flowise node process (command line containing flowise/pyodide) spawning cmd, PowerShell, bash, sh, wsl or similar interpreters. Under normal operation Flowise never spawns an OS shell, so this parent→child pair is a direct post-exploitation artifact of the CVE-2026-69264 Pyodide js-bridge breakout. Rationale: Anchored on the article's execution primitive: Flowise (node) reaching import('child_process') and cp.execSync, which materialises as node.exe spawning an OS shell. The flowise/pyodide command-line filter scopes to the vulnerable app so the parent binary alone (node) does not over-fire. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://www.cryptika.com/six-flowise-rce-flaws-let-attackers-execute-code-on-ai-workflow-servers/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise Custom Function / Custom Tool node legitimately configured by an operator to shell out
  • Developer running Flowise under nodemon/npm scripts that spawn shells during hot reload
  • Container entrypoint wrappers where node execs sh for health checks
  • Legitimate use of a Flowise 'Execute Command' style community node
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("nodemon","npm-cli.js","healthcheck","docker-entrypoint"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — recon (whoami/id/hostname), download (curl/wget), or reverse shell strongly confirm RCE; capture the parent node command line and the DeviceName. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node process, and take the Flowise instance offline pending patch to >=3.1.3. 3) Hunt: enumerate all chatflows on the instance for CSVAgent nodes with crafted csvFile/read_pickle payloads, review /api/v1/prediction access logs for the triggering request (UC1), and check for persistence, dropped files, and outbound C2 from the node process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flowise","pyodide")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","dash","wsl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flowise","pyodide")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh.exe","dash","wsl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise Node process burst-spawning shell/recon children within seconds (post-RCE) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the Flowise node process spawns two or more shell/recon interpreter children inside a 2-second window — the process-tree explosion that follows a successful CSVAgent Pyodide breakout. Uses a temporal count threshold to separate a scripted RCE chain from a single benign shell-out. Rationale: Distinct pivot from UC2: temporal count threshold on the node process. The article's PoC chains multiple OS actions (import, write, execSync); a burst of >=2 shell/recon children in 2s from a flowise-tagged node parent is far higher fidelity than a single spawn. Datadog threshold is applied at rule level. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006 T1059.004

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Node build/test tooling (npm/nodemon) that spins up parallel shells during startup
  • Container orchestration probes issuing rapid sh health checks against the node PID
  • Operator debugging the Flowise host by scripting commands through a custom tool
Suppression filter
| where not (Cmds has_any ("nodemon","docker-entrypoint","healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the Cmds set from the bucket — presence of recon (whoami/id), egress (curl/wget) or a reverse shell confirms exploitation; record DeviceName and the node InitiatingProcessId. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the node process tree, and pull the Flowise instance until it is on >=3.1.3. 3) Hunt: correlate the burst timestamp against /api/v1/prediction access logs (UC1) to identify the source IP and chatflow, then sweep other Flowise hosts for the same node→shell burst pattern and audit chatflows for malicious CSVAgent nodes.

Flowise Node.js process spawning OS shell/recon (Pyodide js-interop RCE sink) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the terminal RCE step of CVE-2026-70470: Pyodide's js module bridge reaches process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync, causing the Flowise Node.js process to spawn a native OS shell or recon binary. On a stock Flowise host the node service never legitimately shells out to cmd.exe/sh to run id/hostname/whoami, so a node parent spawning a command interpreter is a high-fidelity exploitation signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact RCE sink (process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync running 'id && hostname && echo FLOWISE_RCE_CONFIRMED') and the fact that the reachable process is Node.js (Flowise). node -> shell is anomalous on a production Flowise host; the flowise cmdline marker plus recon strings keep FP low. Cross-checked GHSA-52fh-8v99-63c2 and prior CVE-2026-41264 (same Pyodide->child_process sink). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-52fh-8v99-63c2 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3hjv-c53m-58jj • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / npm / yarn build steps spawning cmd.exe or sh during dependency install on developer or CI hosts
  • A legitimate Flowise Custom Tool or ExecuteFlow node designed to shell out to a local script
  • Container health-check or entrypoint wrappers where a node supervisor spawns sh
  • Puppeteer / headless-chrome automation launched from a node process on the same host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","node_modules","webpack","next dev","yarn","npm install","prebuild","puppeteer"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child ProcessCommandLine — recon (id/whoami/hostname/uname), reverse-shell, or download strings confirm exploitation; verify the parent node cmdline is the Flowise service (contains 'flowise'), not a dev/CI build tool. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, kill the offending node process or restart/redeploy the Flowise pod, and pull the public CSV/Airtable-Agent chatflow offline until patched to >=3.1.3. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from the node process after the spawn (C2/exfil), search reverse-proxy logs for the preceding /api/v1/prediction request with homoglyph payload (UC2), and check for dropped files or new persistence written by the node process.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","hostname","whoami","uname")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flowise"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("FLOWISE_RCE_CONFIRMED","hostname","whoami","child_process","/etc/passwd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Unicode homoglyph dunder payload to Flowise /api/v1/prediction (validator bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-70470 defense-evasion step: an HTTP POST to Flowise's /api/v1/prediction endpoint whose body carries Python dunder identifiers built from Mathematical Alphanumeric homoglyphs (U+1D400-U+1D7FF, e.g. __cl𝐚ss__, __b𝐮iltins__) or Cyrillic lookalikes, which slip past the ASCII \b-based validatePythonCodeForDataFrame blacklist. These characters effectively never appear in legitimate chat input, making their presence near double underscores high-signal. Rationale: Uses the article's exact bypass mechanism (Mathematical Bold homoglyphs U+1D400-U+1D7FF such as U+1D41A/U+1D42E forming __class__/__builtins__) against the named endpoint /api/v1/prediction. CIM Web tstats and Defender/Falcon EDR do not carry HTTP POST bodies, so this is expressed as a raw reverse-proxy/WAF search and Sentinel CommonSecurityLog (WAF) regex; leave defender/datadog/falcon empty as their telemetry lacks the request body. Corroborated against GHSA-52fh-8v99-63c2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-52fh-8v99-63c2
ATT&CKT1027 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data-science users pasting genuine mathematical notation (bold/italic Unicode math symbols) into a chat prompt
  • Russian or other Cyrillic-language chat input containing underscores
  • Copy-pasted styled text (LinkedIn/Twitter 'bold' Unicode) submitted as a chat message
  • Authorized penetration testers or vulnerability scanners probing the /api/v1/prediction endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the decoded body — confirm the homoglyph characters sit inside identifier positions adjacent to double underscores (__cl𝐚ss__, __subcl𝐚sses__, __b𝐮iltins__) rather than free prose; note the source IP and chatflowId. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the affected public CSV/Airtable-Agent chatflow offline, and confirm Flowise is upgraded to >=3.1.3. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 on the Flowise host — did the node process spawn a shell within seconds of this request? Search for other requests from the same IP/UA and any prior reconnaissance of the endpoint.

   or (Message has "__" and Message matches regex @"[\x{0400}-\x{04FF}]")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 15 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Entra ID device-code flow authentication (Greatness device-code phishing redemption) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful Entra sign-ins completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant, the specific MFA-bypass primitive Greatness added. Device-code flows are rare and legitimately user-initiated, so a successful device-code sign-in from an unexpected IP/UA is high-signal for an attacker redeeming a phished code. Rationale: Keys on the article's central primitive — the OAuth device authorization grant added to Greatness — via the AuthenticationProcessingDetails "Device Code" marker (canonical Entra sign-in signal for this flow). Covers reviewer suggestions #1/#3 (anomalous device-code initiation + MFA bypass). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code onboarding of shared/kiosk devices, IoT, or conference-room hardware
  • Developers using `az login --use-device-code` or PowerShell/CLI device-code auth
  • Smart-TV / streaming-app style sign-ins to Microsoft 365 apps
  • Break-glass admin using device-code on an unmanaged host
  • Users completing MFA registration on a secondary device
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" and AppDisplayName in ("Microsoft Azure CLI", "Microsoft Azure PowerShell", "Microsoft Authentication Broker"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the IP/UserAgent/geo matches the user's normal pattern and whether a corresponding help-desk or CLI/device onboarding exists; check if the same UPN had an inbound phish with a 'short code' lure in the prior hour. 2) Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), require re-auth, and reset credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot to any device registered by that UPN in the following minutes, new inbox rules, and Graph enumeration of Outlook/Teams/SharePoint (see related UCs) — token validity can persist for weeks.

SigninLogs

| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IsInteractive, ConditionalAccessStatus

M365 authentication from known Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any Entra sign-in or endpoint connection involving the ZeroBEC-observed Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214, which was seen replaying stolen tokens against a victim tenant for over two weeks post-phish. A named IOC makes this alerting-grade. Rationale: Uses the single hard IOC ZeroBEC published (38.248.95.214) confirmed as an active AiTM proxy re-authenticating against a victim tenant weeks after the phish — very low FP as a fixed malicious IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP later reassigned to a benign hoster and reused by a legitimate proxy/VPN
  • Security-team sandbox detonation of the phishing chain from a lab egress that shares the ASN
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation traffic from your own tooling
  • Shared NAT if the malicious host is behind a large provider (rare for /32)
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every UPN authenticated from 38.248.95.214 and the resources/apps accessed; treat each as a candidate token-replay victim. 2) Contain: revoke sign-in sessions and refresh tokens for all matched users, force password reset, and block the IP at the identity provider (named location) and perimeter. 3) Hunt: for each victim, review device registrations, inbox-rule creation, and Graph resource enumeration in the following hours; token lifetime means access may continue absent revocation.

| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs

| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ResultType, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New device registration / PRT generation minutes after a device-code sign-in AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a successful device-code Entra sign-in with an Entra device registration by the same user within 60 minutes — the persistence step Microsoft observed where the actor registers a device to mint a Primary Refresh Token for long-term access. Article-specific temporal chain, not a generic device-join alert. Rationale: Directly encodes Microsoft's reported post-compromise behaviour (register a device within minutes to generate a PRT) chained to the device-code sign-in — the temporal join is what makes it TP-specific rather than routine device enrollment. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new-hire or device-refresh enrollment where the user genuinely used device-code onboarding
  • Autopilot / Intune bulk provisioning windows
  • User enrolling a personal BYOD device after a normal sign-in
  • Help-desk assisted device registration during ticket resolution
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the registered device's OS/name/trust-type and whether it matches corporate managed hardware; verify the sign-in IP against the user's baseline. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable/delete the newly registered device object, revoke the user's tokens (invalidates the PRT), and force credential reset. 3) Hunt: check for inbox-rule creation and Graph enumeration from the same session, and search other users showing device-code sign-in followed by device registration.

Malicious inbox rule created hours after anomalous M365 sign-in AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates an anomalous or device-code Entra sign-in with an Exchange inbox-rule (New/Set-InboxRule) that deletes, moves, or forwards mail, created within 24 hours — the delayed defense-evasion step ZeroBEC/Microsoft observed attackers use to hide traffic and stage exfiltration. Ties two log sources rather than firing on rule creation alone. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific 'wait several hours before setting up malicious inbox rules' tradecraft by joining the rule creation to the preceding device-code/risky sign-in, and filters to hide/forward/delete actions that indicate evasion or BEC staging. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/003/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately creating a forward-to-manager or vacation redirect rule after a normal sign-in
  • Mailbox migration tooling recreating rules
  • Admin-provisioned org-wide transport/inbox rules
  • Power-user building folder-sort rules that move mail to subfolders
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "ForwardTo" and ClientIP in (SigninIP)) or Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage", "Junk")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the exact rule Parameters — external ForwardTo/RedirectTo or delete-on-receipt to 'RSS/Deleted Items' are near-certain malicious; confirm the preceding sign-in was device-code/risky. 2) Contain: remove the inbox rule, revoke user sessions, reset credentials, and add the forwarding target to blocklists. 3) Hunt: enumerate all mailboxes for similar rules created since the campaign start, and review sent-items/Graph pulls for data already exfiltrated.

| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

RingCentral voicemail phishing lure delivered despite SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure (safe-sender bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound voicemail-themed emails impersonating RingCentral that FAILED SPF/DKIM/DMARC yet were Delivered to the inbox — the exact safe-sender-exclusion abuse ZeroBEC documented for Greatness RingCentral campaigns against actual RingCentral customers. Article-specific because the fidelity comes from delivered-despite-auth-failure, not the impersonation alone. Rationale: Combines the article's lure (RingCentral voicemail) with its detection-grade twist — delivered to inbox despite SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure via safe-sender exclusion — which is what distinguishes this from ordinary brand-impersonation phishing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine RingCentral voicemail notifications from a misconfigured connector that fails DMARC
  • Legitimate third-party voicemail-to-email services on the tenant safe-sender list
  • Internal test/phishing-simulation campaigns using RingCentral themes
  • Newsletter/marketing mail from RingCentral that trips DKIM alignment
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain endswith "ringcentral.com" and AuthenticationDetails has "pass")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open EmailUrlInfo for the message, extract the embedded URL and check it against the Greatness .cfd/.one IOC domains; confirm the sender is not a sanctioned RingCentral connector. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide (same cluster), and if any recipient clicked, treat as device-code/AiTM candidate. 3) Hunt: audit and tighten the RingCentral-domain safe-sender/allow-list exclusions (per ZeroBEC guidance), and review UrlClickEvents for click-throughs.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox"
| where SenderFromDomain has "ringcentral" or SenderDisplayName has "RingCentral" or Subject has_any ("voicemail", "voice message", "new voice")
| where AuthenticationDetails has "fail"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

| where AuthenticationDetails has "fail"

Navigation / DNS to Greatness PhaaS phishing infrastructure domains AIDelivery High
Alerts on any email URL, DNS resolution, or endpoint connection to the ZeroBEC-listed Greatness operator domains (hashmashryshl.cfd, hashmashryly.cfd, onlineyoutlook.one, willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd, lookatcreatilcense.one, wbajp.feelingfor.com). Named IOC domains make this alerting-grade infrastructure coverage. Rationale: Ships the pre-extracted Greatness IOC domains across DNS/web/network so any resolution or click is caught regardless of the delivery channel; fixed adversary domains give low FP and cover reviewer suggestion #4 (Greatness infrastructure indicators). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-team sandbox/URL-detonation of the phishing chain from a managed host
  • Threat-intel crawler or proxy pre-fetch of the IOC domains
  • Passive-DNS/monitoring tooling resolving IOCs for enrichment
  • Domain re-registration and repurpose after takedown (stale IOC)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved or navigated to the domain and whether it followed an inbound RingCentral/voicemail lure; check for a subsequent device-code sign-in. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domains at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a full click-through occurred, and revoke the user's tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep EmailUrlInfo/UrlClickEvents tenant-wide for the same domains and pivot on the resolving IP for sibling infrastructure.
let iocDomains = dynamic(["hashmashryshl.cfd","hashmashryly.cfd","onlineyoutlook.one","willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd","lookatcreatilcense.one","wbajp.feelingfor.com","addtorimez.gba","pleasebeatwithlllocliad.gbs"]);
union
( DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any (iocDomains) | project Timestamp, Source="Network", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator=RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName ),
( DeviceEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any (iocDomains) | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceEvent", DeviceName, AccountName, Indicator=RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName )
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocDomains = dynamic(["hashmashryshl.cfd","hashmashryly.cfd","onlineyoutlook.one","willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd","lookatcreatilcense.one","wbajp.feelingfor.com","addtorimez.gba","pleasebeatwithlllocliad.gbs"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (iocDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Kind="DNS" ),
( ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (iocDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=Url, Kind="Web" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-compromise Microsoft Graph enumeration across many M365 resources in minutes AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single principal accessing an unusually broad set of Microsoft 365 resources (Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Exchange, OneDrive) within a short window after token replay — the ZeroBEC-observed post-auth Graph enumeration that follows a Greatness device-code/AiTM compromise. Fan-out on distinct resources, not a single access. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific post-compromise action — replayed tokens enumerating Outlook/Teams/SharePoint/Exchange/OneDrive via Graph — as a per-user resource fan-out within a tight window, which surfaces rapid discovery without alerting on any single normal resource access. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1526/
ATT&CKT1526 T1087.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users / executives genuinely opening many M365 apps at start of day
  • SSO into a suite launcher that pre-authenticates several resources at once
  • Migration or backup service accounts touching many workloads (exclude with the machine-account filter)
  • Mobile devices refreshing tokens for multiple apps after a network change
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountUpn has_any ("svc-", "backup", "sync"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the fan-out originated from a device-code/AiTM sign-in or the Greatness proxy IP, and whether the IP/UA is anomalous for the user. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and reset credentials for the principal; block the source IP if attacker-controlled. 3) Hunt: review what was actually read (mailbox, SharePoint/OneDrive downloads) and correlate with subsequent inbox-rule creation or device registration.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"

| where ResourceCount >= 5   // 5+ distinct M365 resources touched by one user in 10m = enumeration fan-out (baseline P95 ~= 3)
| where Resources has_any ("Office 365 Exchange Online", "Microsoft Teams", "Office 365 SharePoint Online", "Microsoft Graph", "OneDrive")
| order by ResourceCount desc
SigninLogs

| summarize ResourceCount = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)

| where Resources has_any ("Office 365 Exchange Online", "Microsoft Teams", "Office 365 SharePoint Online", "Microsoft Graph", "OneDrive")
| order by ResourceCount desc

Inbound email containing Microsoft device-code / devicelogin URL from external phishing context AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails whose embedded URL points to a Microsoft device-login endpoint (microsoft.com/devicelogin, aka.ms/devicelogin, oauth2 devicecode) — the lure pattern Greatness/Okta describe where the victim is sent to the REAL Microsoft page to enter an attacker-generated short code. Article-specific: the page is legitimate, so the signal is a devicelogin link arriving via external mail. Rationale: Targets the specific device-code phishing lure vector (a link to the genuine Microsoft devicelogin/devicecode endpoint arriving via inbound mail), which the article/Okta call out as the 'short code + plausible reason' trick — covers reviewer suggestion #5. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1621
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT onboarding emails instructing users to complete device-code enrollment
  • Vendor/SaaS docs linking to aka.ms/devicelogin for CLI setup
  • Internal help-desk instructions for smart-device sign-in
  • Security-awareness training emails referencing device-code phishing
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "microsoft.com" and SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourorg.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the sender is external/unexpected and whether the body pressures the user to enter a code 'to listen to a voicemail / view a document'; correlate with UrlClickEvents. 2) Contain: quarantine matching messages tenant-wide; if a recipient clicked and a device-code sign-in followed, revoke tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to any successful device-code Entra sign-in for the recipients within the following hour and to the Greatness IOC domains in the same message.

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Flowise additionalConfig database-path override in vector-upsert API request (CVE-2026-69259) · [LLM] Flowise node runtime spawns shell interpreter (post-exploit command execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Flowise node process writes SQLite DB file to system directory (arbitrary-write RCE primitive) · [LLM] Flowise node process writes to cron / systemd / SSH persistence path · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-69259: Flowise RCE via SQLite Record Manager Node
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Flowise additionalConfig database-path override in vector-upsert API request (CVE-2026-69259) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POSTs to Flowise ingestion endpoints carrying an `additionalConfig` payload that overrides the SQLite `database` path (or supplies TypeORM `entities`/`migrations` for JS-load RCE). This is the exact exploitation primitive for CVE-2026-69259 in FlowiseAI 3.1.2. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable input name `additionalConfig` reaching the Record Manager node via Flowise's `/api/v1/vector/upsert` and document-store ingestion endpoints, correlated with an out-of-tree path (`/etc/`, `/root/`, `.sqlite`) or TypeORM `entities`/`migrations` keys — the confirmed RCE vector. Body inspection requires the proxy/WAF to log request bodies. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/ • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate automation that passes overrideConfig/additionalConfig with a benign in-tree .flowise database path
  • Security scanners / internal pentest hitting the upsert endpoint
  • Developers testing custom Record Manager configs against a staging instance
  • Load-testing tools replaying recorded upsert requests
Suppression filter
| where not (Message has ".flowise" and Message !has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/cron", "/dev/shm", "entities", "migrations"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body for matched events; confirm whether `additionalConfig.database` (or TypeORM `entities`/`migrations`) points outside the `~/.flowise` directory to a system path. Identify the authenticated Flowise user/API key used. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, revoke the Flowise API key, and confirm the Flowise version — upgrade 3.1.2 → 3.1.3+ immediately. 3) Hunt: on the Flowise host pivot to node file-writes and child-process spawns in the following minutes (see companion UCs) to determine if the write/RCE succeeded.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/v1/vector/upsert", "/api/v1/prediction", "/api/v1/document-store")
| where Message has "additionalConfig" or RequestURL has "additionalConfig" or RequestContext has "additionalConfig"
| where Message has_any ("database", "/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/cron", "entities", "migrations", ".sqlite") or RequestURL has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", ".sqlite")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise node process writes SQLite DB file to system directory (arbitrary-write RCE primitive) AIInstallation High
Detects the Flowise node runtime creating a .sqlite/.sqlite3/.db file outside its `.flowise` home in a sensitive system directory — the direct file-write artifact of the CVE-2026-69259 additionalConfig database-path override, which runs as root in the flowiseai/flowise:3.1.2 Docker image. Rationale: Directly grounded in the article's statement that the flaw lets an attacker 'write an SQLite database to an arbitrary filepath, which includes system directories' while the 3.1.2 Docker image 'runs as root'. Keys on node as the writer + SQLite extension + system path, explicitly excluding the legitimate `.flowise` home. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise misconfigured with DATABASE_PATH pointed at a non-default but legitimate directory (e.g. /var/lib/flowise)
  • Backup jobs copying database.sqlite into /root or /var for archival
  • Container image that bind-mounts the SQLite DB to a host system path by design
  • Admin manually relocating the Flowise DB during maintenance
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "/var/lib/flowise" and FolderPath !startswith "/opt/flowise"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath is a genuine system dir (not an approved custom DATABASE_PATH) and capture the file — a SQLite header ('SQLite format 3') in /etc or /root is exploitation. Note InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the writing UID (expect root). 2) Contain: isolate the container/host, snapshot the file for forensics, then delete the planted DB and upgrade Flowise to 3.1.3+. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the preceding upsert API request (web UC) and forward to any cron/persistence file writes or node-spawned shells to scope full RCE.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "nodejs", "node.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".sqlite" or FileName endswith ".sqlite3" or FileName endswith ".db"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/", "/usr/local/sbin/", "/usr/local/bin/", "/dev/shm/")
| where FolderPath !contains ".flowise"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| sort by Timestamp desc

| where ActingProcessName has "node"

| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/", "/usr/local/sbin/", "/usr/local/bin/", "/dev/shm/")

Flowise node process writes to cron / systemd / SSH persistence path AIInstallation High
Detects the Flowise node runtime creating or modifying a file in cron, systemd, init, or SSH authorized_keys directories — the likely means of converting the CVE-2026-69259 root arbitrary-write into code execution and persistence. Rationale: The article states the write targets 'system directories' as root; the canonical way to weaponize a root arbitrary-write into RCE/persistence is dropping a crontab/systemd unit or root authorized_keys. A node process — which should only ever touch its `.flowise` dir — writing to any of these paths is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.002 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Flowise container entrypoint script legitimately templating a systemd unit or cron entry at startup (rare)
  • Configuration-management agent (Ansible/Chef) mislabeled as node writing cron files
  • Admin editing root crontab while a node debug session holds the shell
  • Backup tooling restoring /root/.ssh from a snapshot
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the written file — a cron line, systemd ExecStart, or new SSH key added by node is a confirmed persistence implant; capture the payload command/key. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the malicious cron/unit/key, kill the Flowise container, and rotate any credentials on the box; upgrade to 3.1.3+. 3) Hunt: enumerate all cron.d/systemd/init.d/authorized_keys entries created since the first suspicious upsert request, and check for outbound connections from the payload (node-spawned shell UC).

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| sort by Timestamp desc
