Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1204.002

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'

            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake Adobe and Zoom Updates Install ScreenConnect for Persistent Remote Access

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 17 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an active, multi-wave campaign that employs social engineering lures themed around Adobe and Zoom software updates, business document reviews, and system maintenance utilities to stealthily deploy Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like ConnectWise ScreenConnect. The campaign has been codenamed SMOKE#SCREEN by Securonix Threat

ATT&CKT1027 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1539 T1555.003 T1566 T1566.002
Domainssubscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com solthere.net
IPs207.174.0.143 207.189.11.170

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Powercat fake Xeno loader chain (xeno.exe → AppData javaw.exe → decompiler.exe) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Adobe and Zoom Updates Install ScreenConnect for Persistent Remote Access
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN security-product registry tamper (SmartScreen/Defender) by script host · [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN silent msiexec install of ScreenConnect / ConnectWise Control · [LLM] Powercat stage-3 persistence via HKCU Run 'Display Calibration' → GameDVR payload · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN ScreenConnect relay C2 beacon to attacker IPs / port 8041 · [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN Cloudflare Quick Tunnel C2 (trycloudflare.com staging subdomain) · [LLM] Powercat stage-2 C2 to solthere.net redeem endpoint · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
SMOKE#SCREEN ScreenConnect relay C2 beacon to attacker IPs / port 8041 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the SMOKE#SCREEN staging/relay infrastructure (WsgiDAV stager 207.174.0.143, C# stager 207.189.11.170, and corroborated relay clusters 188.214.34.20 / 169.40.2.68) and ScreenConnect default relay port 8041. This is the persistence-C2 tail of the fake Adobe/Zoom update chain. Rationale: Uses the article's WsgiDAV stager IP (207.174.0.143), the C# payload host (207.189.11.170) and the ScreenConnect relay port 8041; the two additional relay IPs and the port were confirmed by the GuardianMSSP and SC Media re-analysis of the same Securonix report, so they meet the second-source bar. Cross-checked against: • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/08/04/fake-adobe-and-zoom-updates-install-screenconnect-for-persistent-remote-access/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/fake-interactive-zoom-call-leads-to-malicious-screenconnect-download • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/memory-loader-drops-screenconnect
ATT&CKT1219 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organization legitimately runs ConnectWise ScreenConnect on the default relay port 8041 to its own on-prem/cloud relay
  • Security researcher or SOC sandbox intentionally detonating the sample and beaconing to the IOCs
  • Proxy/NAT egress where an internal appliance uses port 8041 for an unrelated service
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment pods that actively probe the IOC IPs
Suppression filter
and not (RemotePort == 8041 and RemoteUrl endswith "<your-managed-screenconnect-relay-fqdn>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal host initiated the flow and the initiating process; a ScreenConnect client with a relay you do not manage on 8041 is confirmation. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the four IOC IPs and port 8041 to untrusted destinations at the egress firewall, and kill/uninstall the unmanaged ScreenConnect client. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the msiexec silent-install chain (UC4), SmartScreen/Defender registry tamper (UC2), and cloudflared tunnel activity (UC3).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("207.174.0.143","207.189.11.170","188.214.34.20","169.40.2.68")
    or (RemotePort == 8041 and RemoteIPType == "Public" and InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl","Client.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("207.174.0.143","207.189.11.170","188.214.34.20","169.40.2.68") or DstPortNumber == 8041
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SMOKE#SCREEN security-product registry tamper (SmartScreen/Defender) by script host AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the batch loader stage that disables SmartScreen and Defender real-time protection via registry edits before running the staged MSI. Scoped to script/console interpreters writing the specific security keys, matching the campaign's nine-step Defender-destruction sequence. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit 'disable AMSI / turn off SmartScreen via Registry / nine-step Defender destruction' step by scoping the exact SmartScreen and Defender RTP value writes to script/console interpreters run by non-machine accounts. Falcon left blank: these non-ASEP registry writes are not covered by the AsepValueUpdate event in the FDR reference. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/news/fake-interactive-zoom-call-leads-to-malicious-screenconnect-download
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin or GPO troubleshooting temporarily disabling SmartScreen on a test host
  • EDR migration project scripting Defender RTP off before installing a third-party AV
  • Software packaging/imaging pipelines that disable SmartScreen for silent installs
  • Legitimate MDM/Intune scripts toggling these keys via powershell
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("CcmExec.exe","IntuneManagementExtension.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "MpPreference -Disable"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a one-liner from cmd/wscript that also disables multiple protections in sequence (SmartScreen + Defender RTP) is high-confidence; a lone GPO-driven change is likely benign. 2) Contain: re-enable the protections, isolate the host, and capture the parent script for analysis. 3) Hunt: look on the same host for a Zone.Identifier-stripped MSI, silent msiexec ScreenConnect install (UC4), and relay beacons (UC1).
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "SmartScreenEnabled" and RegistryValueData =~ "Off")
     or (RegistryValueName =~ "EnableSmartScreen" and RegistryValueData == "0")
     or (RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" and RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable","DisableOnAccessProtection") and RegistryValueData == "1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","reg.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (RegistryValue =~ "SmartScreenEnabled" and RegistryValueData =~ "Off")
     or (RegistryValue =~ "EnableSmartScreen" and RegistryValueData == "0")
     or (RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" and RegistryValue in~ ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable") and RegistryValueData == "1")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","reg.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SMOKE#SCREEN Cloudflare Quick Tunnel C2 (trycloudflare.com staging subdomain) AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network activity to the SMOKE#SCREEN Cloudflare Quick Tunnel used by MemoryLoader.cs (subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com) and, more broadly, first-party non-browser processes reaching any *.trycloudflare.com ephemeral tunnel. Rationale: The exact tunnel subdomain (subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com) is a hard IOC named in the article and the staging server was confirmed to run cloudflared.exe; the broader clause flags first-time non-browser egress to trycloudflare.com without blanket-allowlisting the CDN. Zscaler's MemoryLoader write-up independently confirms the Quick Tunnel usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/memory-loader-drops-screenconnect • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/08/04/fake-adobe-and-zoom-updates-install-screenconnect-for-persistent-remote-access/
ATT&CKT1572 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using Cloudflare Tunnel / cloudflared to expose a local dev service
  • A user visiting a benign site hosted behind a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel in a browser
  • Security testing of trycloudflare tunnels by internal red team
  • IT using trycloudflare for temporary remote support demos
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cloudflared.exe") and RemoteUrl has "subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: the exact subdomain is a direct hit — treat as confirmed; for generic *.trycloudflare.com, check the initiating process (a non-browser like a .NET loader, wscript, or an MSI-dropped binary is high-signal). 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy, isolate the host, and capture the initiating binary (likely the MemoryLoader .NET stager). 3) Hunt: correlate with cloudflared.exe execution, the ScreenConnect relay beacon (UC1), and the silent MSI install (UC4) on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com"
    or (RemoteUrl endswith "trycloudflare.com" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","cloudflared.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has "trycloudflare.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SMOKE#SCREEN silent msiexec install of ScreenConnect / ConnectWise Control AIInstallation Medium
Hunts msiexec.exe launched with silent flags (/quiet, /qn, /passive) that spawns a ScreenConnect/ConnectWise Control client binary — the RMM-abuse install step common to every SMOKE#SCREEN lure once the MSI's Zone.Identifier ADS is stripped. Rationale: Encodes the corroborated 'msiexec /quiet or /passive followed by ScreenConnect binary execution' behaviour, keyed on the ConnectWise product/company version metadata so renamed binaries still match. Kept at hunting tier because managed RMM deployments use the same shape — pair with the unknown-relay context from UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/08/04/fake-adobe-and-zoom-updates-install-screenconnect-for-persistent-remote-access/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/fake-interactive-zoom-call-leads-to-malicious-screenconnect-download
ATT&CKT1219 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT deploying ScreenConnect/ConnectWise agents silently via RMM or SCCM
  • MSP onboarding a managed endpoint with the sanctioned relay
  • Software-packaging test lab installing ConnectWise for evaluation
  • Self-service ScreenConnect reinstall by an authorized support technician
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "<your-sanctioned-screenconnect-instance-id>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the ScreenConnect relay/instance from the installed config and compare to your sanctioned relay allowlist — an unknown relay (esp. on 8041 to UC1 IPs) confirms malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, uninstall the unmanaged agent, block the relay. 3) Hunt: look for the preceding SmartScreen/Defender tamper (UC2), Zone.Identifier removal on the source MSI, and the delivery lure (Dropbox/trycloudflare, UC3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/quiet","/qn","/passive")
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl")
     or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWise Control")
     or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ConnectWise"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("/quiet","/qn","/passive")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Powercat fake Xeno loader chain (xeno.exe → AppData javaw.exe → decompiler.exe) AIDelivery High
Hunts the Bitdefender/ThreatLocker-tracked Powercat infection chain delivered via fake Xeno Roblox executor: a xeno.exe first stage that extracts a bundled JRE and runs javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin, then launches an Allatori-obfuscated JAR masquerading as decompiler.exe. Rationale: Uses the article's named stages (xeno.exe, decompiler.exe) plus the Bitdefender/BleepingComputer-confirmed bundled-JRE path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe; a decompiler.exe that is actually a JAR and a Java runtime under a user AppData path are both strongly anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/ • https://www.threatlocker.com/blog/powercat-malware-campaign-fake-game-cheats-deliver-infostealer-targeting-discord-roblox-and-crypto-wallets
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer with a portable/embedded JRE under AppData running javaw.exe for a legitimate tool
  • A build/CI tool named decompiler.exe used by reverse-engineering staff
  • Minecraft/modding launchers that bundle their own JRE in AppData
  • Portable Java IDE plugins launched from a user profile
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("minecraftlauncher.exe","javaw.exe") and FolderPath has @"\.minecraft\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the javaw.exe path is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin and check for a sibling XenoIcon.jpg (key file) and decompiler.exe JAR; hash the parent xeno.exe. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the java processes, and remove the AppData\Java staging and the GameDVR payload directory. 3) Hunt: pivot to solthere.net C2 (UC6) and the 'Display Calibration' Run-key persistence (UC7), then scope credential/wallet-theft on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "javaw.exe" and FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "xeno.exe"
     or FileName =~ "decompiler.exe"
     or (FileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "decompiler")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "javaw.exe" and ActingProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\")
     or ParentProcessName has "xeno.exe"
     or ActingProcessName has "decompiler.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Powercat stage-2 C2 to solthere.net redeem endpoint AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network activity to the Powercat stage-2 command-and-control domain solthere.net (observed path /api/v1/redeem for pulling the next-stage payload with an AES+Base64 key). Any internal host resolving this domain is a strong Powercat indicator. Rationale: solthere.net is the article's named Powercat C2 domain, independently confirmed by Bitdefender (redeem endpoint /api/v1/redeem) and BleepingComputer; a bare domain match on a rarely-benign infrastructure name is high-fidelity and alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or analyst VM detonating the sample and resolving the C2
  • Security scanner/crawler pre-fetching IOC domains for enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging a blocked lookup (still worth reviewing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and initiating process — javaw.exe from an AppData JRE (UC5) confirms Powercat. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block solthere.net at protective DNS, isolate the host, and terminate the java stealer processes. 3) Hunt: check for the 'Display Calibration' Run key (UC7), the GameDVR payload directory, and browser/wallet/Discord credential access indicative of stage-3 theft.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "solthere.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "solthere.net"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Powercat stage-3 persistence via HKCU Run 'Display Calibration' → GameDVR payload AIInstallation High
Hunts the Powercat stage-3 persistence mechanism: an HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run value named 'Display Calibration' (or any Run value pointing into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR) that auto-runs the fake-named DLL payload at logon. Rationale: Bitdefender confirmed the exact persistence artifact: HKCU\...\Run value 'Display Calibration' pointing at a fake DLL in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR. The masquerading value name plus the GameDVR path make this a single-event, near-zero-FP persistence detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate display-calibration utility that genuinely registers a Run entry (rare; verify the target path is not GameDVR)
  • GameDVR/Xbox Game Bar legitimately writing to its own directory (but not via a Run key with this value name)
  • Endpoint-management tooling seeding benign Run keys during imaging
Suppression filter
| where RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR\" or RegistryValueName =~ "Display Calibration"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData — a Run value named 'Display Calibration' launching a DLL from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR (typically via rundll32/regsvr32) is confirmed Powercat. 2) Contain: delete the Run value, isolate the host, and remove the GameDVR payload; reset credentials for browser/Discord/crypto-wallet apps that may have been harvested. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC5 (loader chain) and UC6 (solthere.net C2) and sweep other gaming endpoints for the same Run value.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Display Calibration"
     or RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Display Calibration"
     or RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"

`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent

Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-04 16 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Nearly half of C2 malware bypasses DNS by connecting directly to IP addresses. Zero trust IP enforcement secures networks against these threats. The post Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phorpiex dropper D2IP payload retrieval from 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SectopRAT in-browser proxy /churl traffic mirroring to attacker IPs · [LLM] Hardcoded WebSocket backdoor to 154.92.19.71:39989 (no DNS) · [LLM] ZT-IP hunt: direct-to-IP egress with no preceding DNS resolution · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Custom \GET obfuscated exfiltration to 18.228.188.56 / SHA256-tracked sample · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phorpiex dropper D2IP payload retrieval from 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts direct-to-IP HTTP GETs to the Phorpiex/Trik staging host 178.16.54.109, which serves loaders (st.exe, 32.exe/64.exe, twizt.exe, xmrig.exe) and staged config paths (/1../6, /sex/k/n.txt, /new.php). Article-specific because the IP is a confirmed long-running Phorpiex delivery node contacted with no preceding DNS query. Rationale: IP 178.16.54.109 is a confirmed Phorpiex C2/loader host (corroborated by Bitsight and executemalware IOC repo serving 32.exe/64.exe/twizt.exe/xmrig.exe), contacted D2IP with no DNS — a high-fidelity, low-FP anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/ransomware-twizt-inside-phorpiex-botnet • https://github.com/executemalware/Malware-IOCs/blob/main/2024-03-28%20Phorpiex%20IOCs • https://otx.alienvault.com/pulse/606aea55d76b8a0aeccfa377
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/sandbox VM detonating samples against the C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IP
  • Honeypot or deception host beaconing to the IP by design
  • Shared-hosting reuse if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant (validate WHOIS/timeframe)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\SandBox\", @"\Analysis\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and its SHA256; pull any file written from the host (st.exe/windrv.exe/sysmgnrsv.exe) via DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block 178.16.54.109 at egress, and quarantine the dropped loader. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256 org-wide, XMRig persistence, and Run-key/service autoruns pointing at %userprofile% driver-look-alike names.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "178.16.54.109"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "178.16.54.109"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SectopRAT in-browser proxy /churl traffic mirroring to attacker IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts SectopRAT (ArechClient2) in-browser proxy beacons to 87.120.107.33 and 194.76.227.94, and the /churl endpoint that relays every visited URL (including authenticated session pages) to the operator. Article-specific because two distinct actors deployed the same family against education using these exact IPs and the /churl proxy path. Rationale: Two named SectopRAT proxy IPs plus the malware-specific /churl relay path give an IP-and-path double anchor; SectopRAT's browser-proxy/BrowserLogging capability is corroborated by Darktrace/G DATA write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/not-your-average-rodent-darktraces-mitigation-of-the-sectop-remote-access-trojan-rat • https://www.gdatasoftware.com/blog/2021/02/36633-new-version-adds-encrypted-communication
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1185 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal API that happens to expose a /churl path (validate against the named IPs)
  • Corporate forward-proxy appliance whose logs mirror URLs (matches /churl only if such a path exists internally)
  • Sandbox detonation of SectopRAT samples by the SOC
  • IP reassignment on shared hosting after the campaign window
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process holding the socket (SectopRAT often injects into or masquerades as a browser/.NET host) and capture its SHA256; review /churl payloads for exfiltrated session URLs. 2) Contain: isolate host, block both IPs, force-reset credentials for any authenticated sessions seen relayed. 3) Hunt: search DeviceProcessEvents for the injecting .NET binary, secondary desktop creation, and other hosts beaconing to either IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94") or RemoteUrl has "/churl"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94") or RequestURL has "/churl"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Custom \GET obfuscated exfiltration to 18.228.188.56 / SHA256-tracked sample AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the persistent \GET (backslash-GET) exfiltration campaign: a malformed HTTP method followed by a 250–666 char structured-encoded blob, beaconing to Brazil-cloud IP 18.228.188.56 with rotating ports. Anchored on the named IP and the disassembled sample hash so it survives the actor's IP/port rotation OpSec. Rationale: Dual anchor: the named C2 IP 18.228.188.56 plus the disassembled sample SHA256 cc43cd… — the hash survives the campaign's documented IP/port rotation, and the \GET method string catches proxy-visible variants. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workload hosted in the same AWS sa-east-1 (Brazil) range if the IP is reassigned post-campaign
  • Proxy that URL-encodes methods and false-matches on a backslash before GET
  • SOC malware detonation of the tracked sample
  • Vulnerability scanner malforming HTTP methods against the host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process matches SHA256 cc43cd… and inspect SentBytes / the encoded blob length (250–666 chars) for exfil volume. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the IP, and preserve the process binary for the encoding-scheme keys noted in the article. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 across all hosts, look for the same 250–666 char \GET pattern to other rotating IPs/ports, and scope impacted sectors (gov/airline/university assets).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "18.228.188.56"
   or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationIP == "18.228.188.56" or RequestMethod contains "\\GET"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestMethod, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, SentBytes, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hardcoded WebSocket backdoor to 154.92.19.71:39989 (no DNS) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the backdoor that opens a WebSocket (wss) directly to the Unicode-hardcoded C2 154.92.19.71 on non-standard port 39989 with zero preceding DNS. Article-specific via the exact IP+port pair extracted from the binary via Ghidra. Rationale: Exact IP+port pair (154.92.19.71:39989) reverse-engineered from the binary as a hardcoded Unicode wss:// string; the non-standard high port plus D2IP makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1071 T1571 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app legitimately using port 39989 to an unrelated host (excluded by the exact IP match)
  • SOC sandbox detonation of the backdoor
  • Deception/honeypot beacon to the IP
  • IP reassignment after the campaign window
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process opening the socket and its SHA256/parent; confirm no DNS query preceded the connection. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 154.92.19.71:39989 at egress, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: extract other hardcoded Unicode IP strings from the sample, sweep for the same binary hash and any other high-port D2IP beacons org-wide.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "154.92.19.71" and RemotePort == 39989
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "154.92.19.71" and DestinationPort == 39989
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ZT-IP hunt: direct-to-IP egress with no preceding DNS resolution AICommand & Control Medium
Encodes the article's zero-trust-IP method — surfacing outbound public-IP connections that carry no resolved domain context (raw IP, no preceding DNS), initiated by non-browser processes. This is how Unit 42 surfaced the Phorpiex, \GET and SectopRAT infrastructure; it is a broad hunting sweep for new D2IP C2 beyond the named IOCs. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's ZT-IP thesis (RemoteUrl empty + public IP = no sanctioning DNS response) and prioritises the five named C2 IPs while surfacing new D2IP infrastructure; scoped to non-browser processes and a burst floor to manage the acknowledged high FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1071 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • NTP/time sync and OS telemetry that legitimately dial IPs directly
  • IP-literal CDN/anycast endpoints (some app updaters, game clients)
  • Monitoring/EDR agents beaconing to hardcoded management IPs
  • P2P/collaboration apps (WebRTC, torrent) using direct-IP mesh
  • Software licensing checks that connect by IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","ntoskrnl.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","w3wp.exe") and RemotePort !in (123, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by the KnownBad flag first, then by rare process+IP pairs; pull the initiating binary's SHA256 and signer. 2) Contain: for any KnownC2 or unsigned/rare binary, isolate the host and block the IP. 3) Hunt: baseline the process→IP pairs over 30 days, promote persistent unexplained D2IP beacons to alerting, and cross-check destinations against threat intel.
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe"]);
let KnownC2 = dynamic(["178.16.54.109","18.228.188.56","87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94","154.92.19.71"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isempty(RemoteUrl)                       // no domain context => direct-to-IP (ZT-IP)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (Browsers)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName)
          by RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| extend KnownBad = RemoteIP in (KnownC2)
| where KnownBad or Conns > 20                   // 20 = burst floor to cut one-off IP checks
| order by KnownBad desc, FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
